new_statements.quote: Stress is unmarked but always occurs on the first syllable of bisyllabic words and on the second last syllable of words of more than two syllables, e.g. 'ɡoɡo many, go'ɡome yam (sp.), 'ɡoɡolelevagi very many.

new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened, PDF p.3 = printed p.109 (rendered and read on the page image). §1.21 Orthography reads: 'Stress is unmarked but always occurs on the first syllable of bisyllabic words and on the second last syllable of words of more than two syllables, e.g. 'gogo many, go'gome yam (sp.), 'gogolelevagi very many.' Verbatim apart from the glyph: the print uses a hooked-g letter for the velar fricative where the reader wrote ɡ. The third example does carry an initial mark on the page ('gogolelevagi), as the reader noted. Reading fixed: penultimate syllable is right (first syllable of a disyllable is its penult; all longer words penult). Relation 'contradicts' is right: the catalog string stress placem…
new_statements.relation_note: Catalog (StressTyp2) gives stress placement coded per word length as 10 100 1010 10010 100010 (1 = a stressed syllable), i.e. primary stress on the initial syllable with a second mark on the penult from four syllables up. Kolia puts the (only) stress on the penult: for disyllables both agree (initial = penult), but for trisyllables the catalog has 100 and Kolia predicts 010, and for longer words the catalog's primary is initial while Kolia's is penultimate. Kolia describes only the Balawaia dialect.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Balawaia dialect (Tauruba village): stress on the first syllable of disyllables and on the penult of longer words, i.e. penultimate stress throughout (the first syllable of a disyllable is its penult). No secondary stress mentioned. (In the print the examples use Kolia's hooked-g glyph for the voiced velar fricative, rendered ɡ here.)
new_statements.exceptions: Kolia's own third example, 'ɡoɡolelevagi 'very many', is marked with initial stress although the stated rule predicts penult for a six-syllable word; the word looks like a compound of ɡoɡo 'many' plus lelevagi, so the mark may be the stress of the first element or a slip. No other exceptions stated.
new_statements.identity_note: Kolia 1975 describes the Balawaia dialect of Sinaugoro as spoken in Tauruba village (Rigo sub-district); the Tauberschmidt dictionary and the StressTyp2 record do not name a dialect in the material opened. Dutton 1970 spells the language 'Sinagoro'.

readall_conflicts: The catalog's single record (StressTyp2: stress placement coded per word length as 10 100 1010 10010 (1 = a stressed syllable), primary stress initial, a further mark on the penult from four syllables up) is contradicted by the only explicit statement opened, Kolia 1975 p. 109 on the Balawaia dialect, which puts stress on the first syllable of disyllables and on the penult of all longer words (i.e. penultimate stress). The two agree on disyllables and on a penult stress in 4+-syllable words, but disagree on trisyllables (initial vs penult) and on which syllable is primary in longer words. The listed work, Tauberschmidt's dictionary, is silent in its open (2007) form. The StressTyp2 record presumably rests on Tauberschmidt's 1999 grammar (PL C-143), which is not in the works list and could not be downloaded (sealang.net mirror: connection refused, then certificate failure; two attempts); the conflict cannot be settled from what was opened.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed-strict, word domain, stress placement coded per word length as 10 100 1010 10010 (1 = a stressed syllable): primary initial, secondary penult from four syllables up) rests on the standard reference grammar, Tauberschmidt 1999 PL C-143, which we hold as an open PDF with text layer; the deciding passage was confirmed verbatim at pp.10-11, including five-syllable verb words showing the 10010 shape. Glottolog 5.1 lists only two descriptive works; the full local Glottolog bib (18 entries) has no phonology article, OPD, JIPA piece or dissertation, and Dutton 1970:883 (downloaded) confirms nothing on Sinagoro phonology predates these. The one refinement found: Kolia 1975:109 (downloaded, open PL C-29) gives the Balawaia dialect penultimate stress in words of three or more syllables (go'gome) against Tauberschmidt's initial stress on Saroa trisyllables; this is a different dialect in a one-sentence sketch remark and does not outrank
